case_name: State Of Jammu & Kashmir v Triloki Nath Khosa & Ors.
facts:
The Judgment of A.
N.
RAY, C.
J.
D.
G.
PALEKAR and Y.
V.
CHANDRACHUD J.J.
was delivered by Chandrachud, J.
If persons drawn from different sources are integrated into one class, can they' be classified for purposes of promotion on the basis of their educational qualifications?

Respondents, who are Diploma Holders in Engineering, filed in the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir a petition u/art.
226 of the Constitution to challenge the validity of certain Service Rules framed by the Government of Jammu and Kashmir.

The respondents contended that under the rules of 1939, Assistant Engineers were entitled to be promoted to the higher cadre on the basis of their merit and record and no distinction was made between degree-holders and diploma holders for the purposes of such promotion.

Respondents further contended that once the Government appointed candidates with different academic or technical qualifications to the same cadre, having the same, pay scale and similar duties, such candidates would form one class and they cannot be further classified for purposes of promotion on the basis of their educational qualifications.
issues: Can persons drawn from different sources be classified for purposes of promotion on the basis of their educational qualifications?
Is the discrimination made by the impugned rules between degree-holders and diploma-holders arbitrary and capricious?

Is the classification of employees based on educational qualifications violative of arts.
14 and 16 of the Constitution?
petitioner_arguments: It was within the competence of the Government to grant a higher pay scale to persons with higher educational qualifications.

Under the Rules of 1968 a higher slab of pay was sanctioned for Assistant Engineers with higher educational qualifications and the qualification Bar was imposed so as to exclude diploma-holders, with a view to ensuring administrative efficiency in the Engineering service.
Classification, for purposes of promotion, on the basis of educational qualifications has an intelligible differentia and was therefore not violative of the constitutional provisions of equality.
respondent_arguments: Neither at the time of appointment to the post of Assistant Engineers nor for the purposes of promotion to the post of Divisional Engineers , was any distinction made by the rules of 1939 between diploma holders and degree-holders;
There is in the instant case no nexus between the classification and the object sought to be achieved thereby and in fact the classification defeats that object;

Having regard to the fact that from 1939 to 1970 holders of Diplomas and Degrees were treated alike, the onus lay heavily on the appellants to prove the necessity for differentiating between the two, which onus was not discharged on the record -of the case;

If the object of the classification was the attainment of efficiency, the Government could have achieved that object, and perhaps in a better measure.
by making talent, experience and efficiency as criteria for determining promotional opportunities.
court_reasoning: The Division Bench held that though it was open to the Government to make a reasonable classification of its employees, where the employees were grouped together and integrated into one unit without reference to their qualifications, they formed a single class in spite of initial disparity in behalf of their educational qualifications and no discrimination could thereafter be made between them on the basis of such qualifications;
The main contention of the respondents was that once there is a class of equals no discrimination can be made among them on any ground whatsoever.

In the alternative, Mr.
Gupte contended, possession of a degree qualification was not a reasonable basis for segregating degree-holders and diploma-holders into water tight compartments.
holding: The correctness of that view is challenged by the State of Jammu and Kashmir in this appeal by special leave.

The impugned rules were violative of arts.
14 and 16 of the Constitution.
The classification made under the Rules of 1968 between diploma-holders and degree-holders was unconstitutional.
